title: Designing and Investigating 3D-Engineered RRAM Devices for Realistic In Situ Electron Microscopy Studies
content: Resistive random access memory (RRAM) is a promising candidate for next-generation non-volatile memory and analog computing, owing to its adaptability in electrode architectures, oxide compositions, and 3D device designs capable of mimicking synaptic plasticity for logic and neuromorphic operations [1]. However, ensuring that in situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) observations remain representative of bulk-scale device behaviour requires a carefully tailored fabrication and characterization approach. To address this challenge, we have developed a fabrication and preparation workflow that begins with engineering the device stack—compromising electrodes, a switching layer, and a controlled microstructure—to confine resistive filaments at specific grain boundaries while preserving the overall electrical performance [2–4]. Following device fabrication, lamella preparation is performed using a weld-free focused ion beam (FIB) technique to prevent the introduction of short-circuit pathways [5].
